title: 7 Best Impact Drivers (2026): One for Every Battery Platform
description: The Milwaukee M18 FUEL 2953-20 is the best impact driver overall; the Ryobi PBLID02, rated 2,200 in-lbs, is the value pick. 7 brushless drivers by platform.
dek: The Milwaukee M18 FUEL 2953-20 is the best impact driver overall; the Ryobi PBLID02, rated 2,200 in-lbs, is the value pick.
intro: Seven brushless impact drivers from Milwaukee, DeWalt, Makita, Ryobi and Bosch, each matched to a job and a battery platform, with the specs the makers publish.

The best impact driver for most people is a brushless 18V or 20V model with at least three speed settings, on the same batteries as your drill. Our overall pick is the Milwaukee M18 FUEL 2953-20; DeWalt owners should get the DCF845, and the Ryobi PBLID02 is the value buy.
quickAnswer: The best impact driver for most people is a brushless 18V or 20V model with at least three speed or mode settings, on the same battery platform as your drill. Our overall pick is the Milwaukee M18 FUEL 2953-20, because it pairs very high rated output with a short head and four drive modes, including one designed for self-tapping screws. If you are on DeWalt, the DCF845 is the full-power choice and the Atomic DCF850 is the compact one. For value, the Ryobi PBLID02 gives you four modes and a brushless motor for noticeably less money.

sections.h: The 7 Best Impact Drivers in 2026 at a Glance

blocks.p: Makita owners should buy the XDT16, which has the finest speed control here. The Milwaukee M12 FUEL 3453-20 is our 12V pick for tight spaces and all-day carry, and the Bosch GDR18V-1860CN is the one to add if you already own Bosch batteries.

We have not bench-tested these tools. Specs come from each maker's published figures and, where a maker's page was incomplete, from retailer and reviewer spec tables that match it. The judgments reflect how each class of driver behaves in normal use and what owners commonly report. Every torque figure is labeled with the brand that measured it, because torque ratings are not comparable across brands, a point we explain in the buying guide below.

As with drills, the battery is the real purchase. If you already own a drill, buy the impact driver that fits its batteries. If you are starting from scratch, our [Milwaukee vs DeWalt](/milwaukee-vs-dewalt/) comparison will help you pick a platform, and our [best cordless drill](/best-cordless-drill/) guide picks the matching drill for each one.

sections.h: Impact Driver vs Drill: What Is the Difference?

blocks.p: An impact driver looks like a short drill, but it works very differently. Instead of a three-jaw chuck it has a 1/4-inch hex quick-release collet that accepts hex-shank bits. Inside, a spring-loaded hammer strikes an anvil many times per second whenever the fastener resists, adding sharp rotational blows to the motor's steady torque. That is why an impact driver can drive a 3-inch screw into dense lumber with little wrist strain, while a drill would stall or twist in your hand.

A drill/driver has a clutch that slips at a set torque, which makes it the better tool for repeatable screw depth in soft materials and for drilling accurate holes with round-shank bits. An impact driver has no clutch, so on small screws and soft materials it is easy to overdrive, strip or snap fasteners unless the tool has low-speed modes. The best modern drivers, like most picks here, solve much of that with speed settings.

Impact drivers are also louder, and the hammering makes them less precise when drilling. You can drill with hex-shank bits, and for small pilot holes that works fine, but for clean, accurate holes, large spade bits or hole saws, the drill is the right tool. Our [best cordless drill](/best-cordless-drill/) guide covers drills in detail.

So which should you buy? If you can only have one tool, a drill/driver is more versatile. If you build decks, fences, sheds or furniture, drive structural screws or lag bolts, or do a lot of repetitive fastening, an impact driver will save time and wrists, and owning both is the standard setup. A combo kit with a drill and impact driver on one platform is usually the best value in cordless tools.
THE RULE
Drive with the impact, drill with the drill.
Keep a drill bit in the drill and a driver bit in the impact driver, and you will rarely need to swap. The impact handles long screws and lags; the drill handles holes and delicate fastening.

The table lines up the seven picks on the specs makers publish. The torque column is each brand's own rating, measured by its own method, so compare those numbers within a brand rather than across brands. Speed, impact rate, modes and size are more reliable for cross-brand comparisons.

Notice that the highest torque rating on the list belongs to the Ryobi, which has the lowest top speed. That is not a contradiction; it is a reminder that each brand measures torque differently and that headline torque does not predict driving speed. Drivers from the big pro brands tend to emphasize speed and impact rate, which shape how fast a screw goes in, as much as torque, which mostly matters on large lags.

The two DeWalt picks share a torque rating but differ in length and top speed, which is exactly the trade-off you are choosing between: the DCF845 for power and pace, the DCF850 for size. For most homeowners either is more than enough.

blocks.h3: Why torque ratings are not comparable

blocks.p: Impact driver torque is measured on a fastener being struck repeatedly, which makes it harder to test consistently than steady motor torque. Brands use their own internal methods and rarely publish the details, including what joint, battery and duration they used. Milwaukee, DeWalt, Makita, Ryobi and Bosch all quote in-lbs, but the numbers are not the result of one shared test. So the Ryobi's 2,200 in-lbs does not mean it out-drives Milwaukee's 2,000 in-lbs, and Makita's 1,600 in-lbs does not mean it is the weakest tool here. Use torque only to compare drivers within one brand.

Top RPM and impacts per minute shape how fast a screw goes in, and they are reported more consistently than torque. Most 18V flagships run around 3,200 to 3,900 RPM. More valuable still are speed settings or modes. A low mode lets you drive small screws without snapping them; a self-tapping or assist mode eases off once a screw starts in metal. Three settings is the minimum we would accept; four is better.

A short head matters more than you might expect. Between studs, inside a cabinet or under a sink, an extra inch decides whether the tool fits square to the screw. The DeWalt DCF850 is under 4 inches; the Milwaukee 2953-20 is 4.47 inches. Weight matters for overhead work and belt carry. Note that makers quote weight differently, sometimes bare and sometimes with a battery, so compare like with like.

All picks here are brushless, which gives better runtime and longevity than older brushed models. Every one uses a 1/4-inch hex quick-release collet. Check that it ejects bits easily and holds them without wobble; owners commonly mention collet feel in reviews, and it is a sign of overall build quality.

sections.h: Match the Impact Driver to Your Drill

blocks.p: The single most important rule when buying an impact driver is to buy it on the same battery platform as your drill. Batteries and chargers are the expensive part, and two tools sharing a set of packs is far cheaper than two separate systems. If you own a Milwaukee M18 drill, buy the 2953-20. If you own DeWalt 20V MAX, buy the DCF845 or DCF850. Makita LXT owners should buy the XDT16, Ryobi owners the PBLID02, and Bosch owners the GDR18V-1860CN.

If you are buying both tools at once, a combo kit is usually the best deal, but check which impact driver is in it. Combo kits sometimes include an older or lower-tier driver to hit a price, so compare the model number against the picks here. Our [Milwaukee vs DeWalt](/milwaukee-vs-dewalt/) guide compares what you get across the two biggest pro platforms, including battery sizes and warranty.

Ryobi ONE+ is the platform for homeowners who want many tools for little money; our [Ryobi tools review](/ryobi-tools-review/) covers where it is strong and where it falls short. Milwaukee and DeWalt are the long-term pro choices, and Milwaukee's M12 line adds a second, compact family that is ideal for a 12V drill and impact pair. Makita and Bosch are excellent but smaller in the US.

If you already own a 12V drill and an 18V drill, consider which you reach for most. Many people find the 12V impact driver is the one they use daily, because it is light enough to keep on a belt, and they leave the 18V tools for decks and framing.

sections.h: Bits, Fasteners and Getting Good Results

blocks.p: An impact driver is only as good as the bit in it. Standard screwdriver bits are hard and brittle and will crack under impact blows; use bits labeled impact-rated, which are made to flex slightly and survive. Buy a few of the sizes you use most, usually #2 Phillips, T25 Torx and square drive, because they wear out and a worn bit cams out and strips screw heads.

Fastener choice matters too. Torx and square-drive screws grip far better than Phillips under an impact driver, which is why most deck and structural screws use them. For lag screws, use a hex socket adapter, drill a pilot hole sized to the screw's root diameter, and drive in a lower mode until the head seats, then stop. Over-tightening a lag with an impact driver is easy and can strip the wood fibers.

For delicate work, such as cabinet hardware, hinges or small screws into softwood, use the lowest speed setting and feather the trigger. If a job needs repeatable screw depth in soft material, switch to a drill with a clutch. For machine fasteners where an exact tightness matters, such as lug nuts or engine parts, an impact driver is the wrong tool entirely; use a properly set [torque wrench](/best-torque-wrench/).
Finally, wear hearing protection for long sessions. Impact drivers are loud, and an afternoon of decking adds up. Eye protection is sensible too, since snapped bits and screw heads can fly.

sections.h: 12V or 18V and 20V: Which Do You Need?

blocks.p: A 12V impact driver like the Milwaukee M12 FUEL 3453-20 is smaller and lighter than an 18V model and still has real power. Milwaukee rates it at up to 1,500 in-lbs and lists it at 2 lb, which makes it a pleasure for cabinet installs, electrical work, furniture assembly and general home projects. The trade-off is stamina on heavy work: small batteries and less headroom mean slower progress on long lags and structural screws.

An 18V or 20V driver like the 2953-20 or DCF845 is the right choice for decks, fences, framing, sheds and any project with hundreds of long screws. With a 4.0 or 5.0Ah battery, it will run most of a day of decking. The compact 18V models, like the DCF850, narrow the size gap a lot.

If you only buy one impact driver, make it 18V or 20V on the platform of your drill. If you already have one and work a lot in tight spaces, a 12V driver is a great second tool, and paired with a 12V drill, it makes a light everyday kit.

sections.h: Which Impact Driver Should You Buy?

blocks.p: If you already own batteries, buy that brand's driver from this list: the 2953-20 or 3453-20 for Milwaukee M18 or M12, the DCF845 or DCF850 for DeWalt 20V MAX, the XDT16 for Makita LXT, the PBLID02 for Ryobi ONE+, and the GDR18V-1860CN for Bosch 18V.

If you are starting from scratch, choose a platform first with our [Milwaukee vs DeWalt](/milwaukee-vs-dewalt/) guide, then buy a drill and impact driver together. For long-term pro use, the Milwaukee 2953-20 with the 2903-20 drill, or a DeWalt DCF845 with the DCD800, are both strong pairs. For homeowners on a budget, the Ryobi PBLID02 with the PBLDD02 drill gives you two brushless tools and the widest cheap tool family. For tight spaces, the M12 FUEL pair is hard to beat.

Whatever you buy, use impact-rated bits, keep the low mode for small screws, and let the drill handle the holes. Our [best cordless drill](/best-cordless-drill/) guide covers the other half of the pair.

mistakes: Each maker measures impact torque by its own method and rarely publishes the details. A 2,200 in-lbs rating from one brand does not beat a 2,000 in-lbs rating from another. Compare torque only within one brand, and judge across brands on speed, modes, size and platform.
Using standard bits in an impact driver

Ordinary screwdriver bits are brittle and crack under impact blows, then cam out and strip screw heads. Buy impact-rated bits in the sizes you use most and replace them when the tips round over. They are cheap, and a worn bit wastes screws and time.
Driving small screws on full power

An impact driver has no clutch. On top speed it will snap small screws, strip soft wood and crack trim. Use the lowest mode for small fasteners and cabinet hardware, feather the trigger, or switch to a drill with a clutch when screw depth matters.
Using an impact driver for precise torque

Impact drivers are not torque-controlled tools. Never use one to tighten lug nuts, engine fasteners or anything with a specified torque. Run fasteners down with the driver if you like, then finish with a properly set torque wrench.
Buying a combo kit without checking the driver model

Some combo kits include an older or lower-tier impact driver to hit a price. Check the model number in the listing against current models before you buy. A slightly pricier kit with the current flagship driver is often the better long-term value.
bottomLine: Buy the impact driver that fits your drill's batteries. For Milwaukee that is the M18 FUEL 2953-20, or the M12 FUEL 3453-20 for tight spaces; for DeWalt the DCF845 or the compact Atomic DCF850; for Ryobi the PBLID02, for Makita the XDT16, and for Bosch the GDR18V-1860CN. Ignore cross-brand torque comparisons, use impact-rated bits, keep the low mode for small screws, and let the drill handle the holes. Get those right and any driver on this list will make your next deck or cabinet job faster.

faqs.q: What is the best impact driver for the money?
faqs.a: For most homeowners, the Ryobi PBLID02 offers the best value. It has a brushless motor, four modes including an Assist mode for self-tapping screws, and a rated 2,200 in-lbs of torque, on the ONE+ platform with hundreds of affordable tools. If you are on a pro platform already, the best value is always the driver that fits your existing batteries.

faqs.q: Is an impact driver better than a drill?
faqs.a: It is better at driving long screws, structural fasteners and lag bolts, and it is easier on your wrist. A drill is better at drilling accurate holes, running large bits, and driving small screws to a repeatable depth thanks to its clutch. If you can only buy one, buy a drill; if you build anything, own both.

faqs.q: Can I use an impact driver as a drill?
faqs.a: For small pilot holes with hex-shank drill bits, yes, and it works well. For clean, accurate holes, large spade bits, hole saws or masonry, no. The hammering action makes it less precise, and it cannot hold round-shank bits. Use a drill/driver for real drilling and keep the impact driver for fastening.

faqs.q: How much torque do I need in an impact driver?
faqs.a: Every 18V or 20V driver on this list has enough for deck screws, structural screws and moderate lag bolts. Because each brand rates torque differently, do not shop by headline torque across brands. Look at speed modes, size and platform instead. A 12V driver is enough for cabinets, electrical work and most household projects.

faqs.q: Is Milwaukee or DeWalt better for impact drivers?
faqs.a: Both make excellent impact drivers. Milwaukee's 2953-20 has four drive modes and a short head; DeWalt offers the full-power DCF845 and the very short Atomic DCF850. The bigger decision is the battery platform, which our Milwaukee vs DeWalt guide covers in detail. Buy the driver that matches your drill's batteries.

faqs.q: Do I need special bits for an impact driver?
faqs.a: Yes. Use bits labeled impact-rated, which are designed to survive repeated rotational blows. Standard bits are harder and more brittle and can crack or shatter. You also need hex-shank bits, because the impact driver's 1/4-inch hex collet cannot hold round-shank bits. Torx and square-drive bits grip better than Phillips.

faqs.q: Is a brushless impact driver worth it?
faqs.a: Yes. Brushless motors run cooler, get more work from each battery charge and generally last longer than brushed motors, and they are standard on every current mid-range and pro impact driver. All seven picks here are brushless. A brushed driver is only worth considering at the very cheapest end, for occasional light use.
